about_blocks: Identify the Royalty Account Before Modeling It

The working file begins with the record owner, payor account, county, legal description, lease, unit, well names, products, owner decimal, and the months represented by the latest payment. If a statement combines wells or products, each line remains traceable rather than being rolled into one unexplained monthly number.
Reconcile the Decimal Against the Ownership Story

A division order decimal is an important clue, not a substitute for title. We compare it with the owner's deed or inheritance path, lease royalty, tract fraction, unit allocation, depth or formation limits, reservations, and any recent payor correspondence. A mismatch becomes an open question instead of a convenient assumption.
Read Revenue, Deductions, and Adjustments Line by Line

Gross sales volume, realized price, severance and ad valorem taxes, gathering, compression, processing, transportation, marketing, prior-period adjustments, suspense releases, and recoupments can all change the check. The review separates recurring economics from one-time noise so a temporary spike or shortfall does not control the conversation.
Separate Producing Value From Undeveloped Possibility

Existing wells have production histories, downtime, workovers, operating decisions, decline behavior, and remaining uncertainty. Future locations depend on spacing, permits, operator inventory, capital allocation, offset results, service constraints, commodity outlook, and timing. The buyer's model should keep those two value sources visible.
Compare Offer Terms With the Same Care as the Price

A headline amount belongs beside the interest description, included depths, effective date, title standard, adjustment formula, diligence period, financing condition, deposit, deed warranties, closing date, revenue treatment, and rights reserved by the owner. Those terms determine whether the quoted number describes the same transaction the owner expects.
Close the Interest That Was Actually Reviewed

The final purchase agreement, title schedule, conveyance exhibit, settlement calculation, signer authority, funding condition, recording package, operator or payor notice, and post-closing revenue handoff should match. We keep the operating facts and closing documents connected so a last-minute legal-description or decimal change is not hidden inside paperwork.

situations: Find the Event That Changed the File

The situation is easier to evaluate when the triggering event is explicit. That may be a death, probate filing, trust change, family transfer, new division order, suspended payment, operator acquisition, unsolicited offer, tax need, or a check that no longer resembles the prior months. The review records the date, people, entities, tracts, wells, payors, documents, and unanswered questions attached to that event.
Keep Ownership Questions Separate From Production Questions

In this situation, a title issue can affect who owns the payment while a production issue affects how much the wells generate. A buyer should not use weak production to guess at title, or a title gap to dismiss a well history. We track deed and authority evidence on one side and statements, wells, volumes, prices, deductions, downtime, and operator activity on the other.
Match the Timeline to the Owner's Real Decision

The owner in this situation may be considering a full sale, a partial sale, a retained fraction, a request for more information, or no transaction at all. The review should show which documents are available now, which can be obtained from county or regulatory records, what requires professional title or tax advice, how long an offer remains open, and which facts could change before closing.
interest-types: Name the Economic Right Before Applying a Multiple

The interest can describe a different combination of ownership, executive rights, lease participation, royalty burden, development control, liability, depth, formation, and duration. A buyer needs the deed, lease, assignments, reservations, division order, payor statement, and unit context to decide which cash flows and future rights are actually included.
Trace the Decimal From Tract to Check

For this interest, the owner decimal should be explainable as a chain: ownership fraction, net acreage or tract share, lease royalty or overriding burden, unit allocation, product, and payor setup. The result on a division order may be correct, stale, provisional, or limited to one well. We label which step is documented and which remains assumed.
Write Included and Retained Rights Into the Offer

A proposal for this interest should identify counties, tracts, legal descriptions, wells, units, depths, formations, fractions, and reservations. It should also say whether current receivables, suspense, post-effective-date revenue, audit rights, claims, surface rights, or operating liabilities transfer. The conveyance cannot safely rely on a broader marketing label.
basins: Use Basin Context Without Losing the Tract

The basin provides useful context for target formations, operator behavior, spacing, takeaway, price differentials, service capacity, offset results, and development tempo. The subject royalty still depends on its own legal description, lease, unit, wells, decimal, burdens, production history, and title. A basin story is not a tract schedule.
Separate the Existing Well Deck From Future Inventory

A buyer looking at the basin should show what value is assigned to current production, proved behind-pipe or workover possibilities, permitted locations, and broader undeveloped inventory. Each layer carries different timing, decline, capital, operator, commodity, and execution assumptions. Combining every layer into one per-acre number hides the source of disagreement.
Account for Realized Pricing and Operating Friction

Royalty cash flow in the basin can reflect oil or gas quality, gathering, processing, compression, transportation, marketing, taxes, flaring or curtailment, seasonal access, workovers, shut-ins, ownership changes, and operator accounting adjustments. The review compares the owner's actual statement history with the buyer's modeled net revenue instead of assuming benchmark price reaches the check unchanged.
locations: Build the File From the County Outward

A state review begins with the county, legal description, record owner, deed chain, probate or trust instruments, lease, assignments, pooling or unit records, division orders, operator and payor accounts, regulator well data, and recent check detail. Statewide production headlines can guide questions, but they do not identify the interest being conveyed.
Match State Rules to the Actual Instrument

In each state, recording practice, marital or community-property questions, probate, acknowledgments, transfer documents, regulatory terminology, tax treatment, and operator notice procedures may differ. Those items belong with the owner's attorney, accountant, title professional, and closing team. The buyer's file should flag them early enough that a local requirement does not surface after price and timing are already assumed.
Keep the Payor Trail Current Through Closing

The royalty account may change because of operator acquisitions, payor changes, new wells, revised units, division order updates, suspense, curative work, or a different effective date. The review records which statements and contacts are current, how revenue is handled between signing and closing, and who sends the post-closing ownership or payment notice.
resources: Turn the Guide Into a Royalty-File Check

Each guide should lead to a concrete action: identify a statement field, request a deed or lease, compare a decimal, locate a well, confirm the payor, list a deduction, date an adjustment, label an offer term, or ask the right professional a focused question. A guide is useful when it improves the working file.
Use the Statement as Evidence, Not a Complete Title Opinion

The check detail shows what a payor currently recognizes and how revenue was calculated for particular wells and months. It may not show every tract, depth, reservation, executive right, unpaid period, or title issue. We use it to frame the next document request without presenting payor accounting as a complete ownership conclusion.
Preserve the Date and Source of Every Number

Production, prices, deductions, decimals, permit status, operator plans, and offers change. The file should record the source, date, unit, product, well, period, and whether a figure is gross, net, owner-specific, historical, projected, or estimated. That makes later revisions understandable instead of looking like unexplained valuation swings.
investing: Build the Producing Case From the Revenue Deck

The buyer should begin with well-level sales volumes, products, realized prices, taxes, deductions, owner decimals, downtime, adjustments, and the dates covered by the statement history. Gross regulatory production and net owner revenue are not interchangeable. The bridge between them should show unit allocation, lease burden, product mix, post-production costs, and the owner's actual payor setup. A dated reconciliation also keeps a suspense release or prior-period correction from masquerading as ordinary monthly cash flow.
Model Decline Without Pretending It Is Mechanical

A decline curve is an informed estimate, not a clock. Completion design, choke strategy, pressure behavior, offset interference, artificial lift, workovers, curtailment, operating practices, data gaps, and changing ownership of the asset can alter the path. The buyer's case should state the history used, forecast start date, decline form, terminal behavior, downtime allowance, and sensitivity range.
Keep Future Development in a Separate Layer

A royalty package may include value for permits, spacing, offset results, undeveloped benches, refracs, recompletions, or operator inventory. Each opportunity needs a formation, location count or probability, working-interest or royalty basis, capital and service context, timing, production shape, price deck, burden, and discount rate. Undeveloped upside should not quietly inflate the producing cash flow or be described as certain.
Stress-Test Price, Differential, and Deductions Independently

A useful review changes benchmark oil or gas price, basin differential, product mix, gathering, compression, processing, transportation, marketing, taxes, and other deductions in separate cases. A buyer may be optimistic on commodity price but conservative on netback, or the reverse. Showing those variables individually makes the offer easier to compare with the owner's recent statements.
Discount the Cash Flow and the Execution Risk

The analysis should identify the forecast periods, discount convention, terminal treatment, title reserve, data uncertainty, operator concentration, development timing, commodity sensitivity, and closing adjustments. The output is a buyer's underwriting case, not an appraisal or investment recommendation. The owner should be able to see which facts are observed, which are modeled, and which could change the final amount.
exchange-1031: Confirm the Exchange Question Before Reshaping the Sale

Before the sale, the owner should ask a qualified intermediary, attorney, and tax adviser whether the relinquished interest, replacement property, taxpayer, vesting, timing, related parties, debt, and proposed structure fit the owner's situation. A mineral buyer can supply accurate transaction facts and dates, but should not promise exchange qualification or choose the owner's tax elections. That advice boundary should remain visible in emails, calendars, draft agreements, and settlement instructions from the first review forward. The file should also record who is responsible for each decision, when that decision is due, and which document carries it into closing.
Keep the Royalty Underwriting File Intact

A possible exchange does not change the need to identify the counties, tracts, interests, wells, depths, formations, fractions, effective date, title standard, adjustment mechanics, and retained rights in the interest being sold. The buyer's production and development assumptions should remain documented even when closing timing or proceeds routing receives extra attention.
Coordinate the Intermediary Before Funds Move

The working file should identify the current owner, proposed seller, purchasing entity, qualified intermediary, escrow or closing agent, legal and tax advisers, assignment language, notice requirements, consideration estimate, expected adjustments, and intended proceeds path. Those parties and documents should be confirmed before the mineral sale closes or funds are released.
Run One Calendar for the Sale and One for the Exchange

An exchange can involve offer expiration, purchase-agreement signing, title review, curative work, adjustment deadlines, deed execution, mineral closing, intermediary assignment, the 45-day identification period, and the 180-day acquisition period. Putting every event on one page helps the owner see where buyer diligence, title work, replacement-property decisions, and adviser approvals can collide.

The owner considering an exchange should understand what happens if the exchange proceeds, changes, or does not occur. The purchase agreement, deed, title schedule, settlement statement, revenue allocation, and buyer funding conditions still need to work as a mineral sale. A backup path should not be interpreted as tax advice, but it prevents unclear exchange assumptions from making the underlying conveyance vague.
